Name: Lean Canvas
Author: Ash Maurya
Key_Concepts: Problem|Solution|Key Metrics|Unfair Advantage|Channels|Cost Structure|Revenue Streams|Value Proposition|Customer Segments
Steps: 1. Start with Customer Segments|2. Define top 3 Problems|3. Write Unique Value Proposition|4. Sketch Solution|5. Identify Channels|6. Define Revenue Streams|7. Map Cost Structure|8. Define Key Metrics|9. State Unfair Advantage
Best_For: First business model draft — test hypotheses before building

Name: Business Model Canvas
Author: Alexander Osterwalder
Key_Concepts: Key Partners|Key Activities|Key Resources|Value Proposition|Customer Relationships|Channels|Customer Segments|Cost Structure|Revenue Streams
Steps: 1. Map all 9 blocks|2. Identify assumptions per block|3. Prioritize riskiest assumptions|4. Design experiments|5. Iterate based on evidence
Best_For: Established business model analysis and pivoting
Decay_Note: Business model patterns shift — review biannually

Name: Mom Test
Author: Rob Fitzpatrick
Key_Concepts: Good questions vs bad|Three rules|Commitment and advancement|Customer conversations
Steps: 1. Never tell them your idea|2. Ask about their life not your concept|3. Talk less listen more|4. Seek facts not opinions|5. Look for commitments|6. Push for specifics
Best_For: Customer validation interviews — avoiding biased feedback

Name: Jobs-to-be-Done
Author: Clayton Christensen
Key_Concepts: Functional jobs|Emotional jobs|Social jobs|Forces of progress|Hiring criteria
Steps: 1. Identify the job customer is hiring for|2. Map functional + emotional + social jobs|3. Understand forces of progress (push/pull/anxiety/inertia)|4. Design solution for the whole job|5. Test with switching interviews
Best_For: Understanding WHY customers buy — beyond features

Name: Bullseye Framework
Author: Gabriel Weinberg
Key_Concepts: 19 channels|Outer ring (brainstorm)|Middle ring (test)|Inner ring (focus)
Steps: 1. Brainstorm all 19 channels (outer ring)|2. Rank by likelihood/cost/scale|3. Test top 3 cheaply (middle ring)|4. Double down on #1 winner (inner ring)|5. Re-run when channel saturates
Best_For: Finding your #1 traction channel from 19 options

Name: ICE Scoring
Author: Sean Ellis
Key_Concepts: Impact (1-10)|Confidence (1-10)|Ease (1-10)|ICE Score = I×C×E
Steps: 1. List all ideas/features/experiments|2. Score Impact 1-10|3. Score Confidence 1-10|4. Score Ease 1-10|5. Calculate I×C×E|6. Rank and execute top items
Best_For: Prioritizing ideas and experiments by ROI

Name: Pirate Metrics (AARRR)
Author: Dave McClure
Key_Concepts: Acquisition|Activation|Retention|Referral|Revenue
Steps: 1. Map each stage of funnel|2. Define key metric per stage|3. Identify biggest drop-off|4. Focus optimization on worst stage|5. Measure improvement weekly
Best_For: Startup funnel metrics — identify and fix weakest stage

Name: Sean Ellis PMF Survey
Author: Sean Ellis
Key_Concepts: How would you feel if you could no longer use this product? Very disappointed|Somewhat disappointed|Not disappointed
Steps: 1. Ask users: How would you feel if you could no longer use [product]?|2. Very disappointed ≥40% = PMF|3. Analyze 'very disappointed' segment profile|4. Build for that segment|5. Re-run monthly
Best_For: Measuring product-market fit quantitatively

Name: Build-Measure-Learn
Author: Eric Ries
Key_Concepts: Hypothesis|Build MVP|Measure data|Learn insight|Iterate or pivot
Steps: 1. State hypothesis clearly|2. Build minimum experiment to test|3. Define success metric BEFORE building|4. Measure results|5. Learn: validate or invalidate|6. Pivot or persevere
Best_For: Core Lean Startup loop for validated learning

Name: Design Thinking
Author: IDEO/Stanford d.school
Key_Concepts: Empathize|Define|Ideate|Prototype|Test
Steps: 1. Empathize with users|2. Define the problem statement|3. Ideate solutions broadly|4. Prototype quickly|5. Test with real users|6. Iterate
Best_For: Human-centered problem solving and innovation

Name: OKR Framework
Author: John Doerr
Key_Concepts: Objectives (qualitative)|Key Results (quantitative)|Alignment|Cadence
Steps: 1. Set 3-5 Objectives per quarter|2. Each Objective gets 3-5 measurable Key Results|3. Score KRs 0.0-1.0|4. Aim for 0.6-0.7 (stretch)|5. Review weekly and quarterly
Best_For: Goal setting and alignment for growing teams

Name: Specific Knowledge × Personal Problem
Author: Naval Ravikant
Key_Concepts: Specific knowledge|Personal problem|Customer zero|Authenticity|Cannot be trained
Steps: 1. What problem do YOU have?|2. What specific knowledge do YOU have that others don't?|3. Is the intersection economically valuable?|4. Are you Customer Zero?|5. Can competitors copy 'being you'?
Best_For: Giantiny Pillar ① — finding ideas from personal pain + unique skills

Name: Counter-Positioning
Author: Hamilton Helmer
Key_Concepts: Business model incumbents can't copy|Self-destructive to copy|Structural moat
Steps: 1. What is your business model?|2. Can big competitors copy it?|3. If yes — would copying hurt their existing business?|4. Basecamp test: would copying your pricing destroy their sales team?|5. If no structural barrier → rethink
Best_For: Giantiny Pillar ② — creating models big players can't copy

Name: Code + Media Leverage
Author: Naval Ravikant
Key_Concepts: Code replaces labor|Media replaces marketing|Zero marginal cost|Permission-less leverage
Steps: 1. Can code automate this task?|2. Can media replace this salesperson?|3. If need >3 people → architecture wrong|4. Prioritize 1-person operable stack|5. Monitor platform risk (<70% single channel)
Best_For: Giantiny Pillar ③ — zero marginal cost levers replace labor

Name: Hook Model
Author: Nir Eyal
Key_Concepts: Trigger (internal/external)|Action|Variable Reward|Investment
Steps: 1. Identify internal trigger (emotion)|2. Simplify action to minimum|3. Design variable rewards|4. Create investment that improves next cycle|5. Test habit-forming loop
Best_For: Building habit-forming products that drive retention

Name: Shape Up
Author: Basecamp
Key_Concepts: Shaping|Betting table|6-week cycles|Fixed time variable scope|Hill charts
Steps: 1. Shape the work (define appetite + boundaries)|2. Bet on shaped projects at betting table|3. Build in 6-week cycles|4. Fixed time variable scope — cut scope NOT time|5. Use hill charts to track progress|6. Cool-down between cycles
Best_For: Product development methodology — fixed time variable scope

Name: Profit-First Framework
Author: Mike Michalowicz
Key_Concepts: Revenue allocation|Profit account|Tax account|Operating expenses|Pay yourself first
Steps: 1. Open separate bank accounts: Profit Tax OpEx Owner|2. Allocate revenue by percentages|3. Profit first — not last|4. Cut expenses to fit profit-first allocation|5. Review quarterly
Best_For: Giantiny Pillar ④ — optimize profit not growth speed

Name: Micro-MOAT Framework
Author: Giantiny Biz
Key_Concepts: Micro-Network Effects (templates/plugins)|Proprietary Micro-Data|Authentic Brand
Steps: 1. Identify which MOAT type fits: Network or Data or Brand|2. Network: open platform for user-generated assets|3. Data: collect niche data competitors can't buy|4. Brand: build personal authentic presence|5. Aim for at least 1 Micro-MOAT by Stage 5
Best_For: Giantiny Pillar ⑤ — defense strategy for solo/small teams

Name: Problem Anatomy — Monkey Problem
Author: IdeaValidator / Astro Teller (Google X)
Keywords: monkey problem,hardest variable,core difficulty,risk assessment,critical assumption,make or break,entry point,validation priority
Key_Concepts: Identify the single hardest variable that decides success or failure|If this one thing fails the entire JTBD collapses|Prioritize solving this BEFORE anything else|Named after Google X: tackle the monkey (hardest part) before building the pedestal
Steps: 1. List all assumptions your idea needs to be true|2. Rank by impact: which one failing kills everything?|3. The top-ranked assumption is your Monkey Problem|4. Design your first experiment to test ONLY this assumption|5. If it fails restructure or pivot before building anything else
Best_For: Pre-idea founders and early validation — forces focus on what truly matters instead of building features

Name: Problem Anatomy — Weakchain Analysis
Author: IdeaValidator / Theory of Constraints
Keywords: weakchain,process friction,break point,entry point,mvp scope,customer journey,pain point mapping,bottleneck,constraint
Key_Concepts: Map the customer current action chain end-to-end|Find the step causing most frustration (they use makeshift solutions)|This broken step is where your MVP should start|Weakchain = your market entry point with least resistance
Steps: 1. Map customer current workflow step by step (5-10 steps)|2. For each step ask: what makeshift solution do they use?|3. Rate each step: friction level 1-10|4. The highest-friction step with a makeshift workaround is your Weakchain|5. Build MVP that replaces ONLY this one step
Best_For: Scoping MVP — prevents over-building by identifying the single highest-impact entry point

Name: Problem Anatomy — Do-Nothing Scenario
Author: IdeaValidator
Keywords: do nothing,nice to have,must solve,urgency,pain severity,inaction cost,status quo,must-have vs nice-to-have
Key_Concepts: Ask: what happens if nobody builds this solution?|If world is still fine = Nice-to-have (avoid)|If real damage in money time or status = Must-solve (proceed)|Forces honest assessment of problem severity|Filters vitamin vs painkiller ideas
Steps: 1. Describe what happens if customer does nothing for 6 months|2. Quantify the damage: dollars lost? hours wasted? reputation hit?|3. If damage is vague or minimal this is a Nice-to-have — iterate on problem|4. If damage is concrete and measurable this is a Must-solve — proceed|5. Use the quantified damage as your sales pitch anchor
Best_For: Killing bad ideas early — most powerful single filter before spending time on validation

Name: Market Timing — Why Now Framework
Author: IdeaValidator / Bill Gross (Idealab)
Keywords: market timing,why now,enabler,technology shift,behavior change,regulatory change,timing,window of opportunity
Key_Concepts: Right idea + wrong timing = failure|Look for 3 types of Enablers: Technology (AI makes it 10x cheaper) Behavior (remote work accepted) Regulatory (GDPR forces new solutions)|Bill Gross research: timing is #1 factor in startup success above team idea and business model|Check Google Trends + funding data + job postings as signals
Steps: 1. Identify technology enabler: what new tech makes this 10x cheaper or faster?|2. Identify behavior enabler: what consumer habit changed recently?|3. Identify regulatory enabler: what new law forces customers to act?|4. Check Google Trends for 5-year search volume trend|5. If search up 50%+ in 12 months AND 2-3 companies just entered AND funding increasing — timing is right
Best_For: Validating that the market is ready NOW not too early or too late

Name: 4-Dimension Impact Assessment
Author: IdeaValidator / Clayton Christensen
Keywords: functional needs,emotional needs,breakthrough ux,billion market,impact assessment,value potential,word of mouth,market size validation
Key_Concepts: Evaluate idea across 4 dimensions simultaneously|Functional: does it get the job done faster?|Emotional: does it reduce anxiety or increase confidence? (Emotions drive word-of-mouth)|Breakthrough UX: is the experience shockingly better than status quo?|Market scale: are enough people willing to pay? (Idea vs Opportunity filter)
Steps: 1. Rate Functional impact 1-10: how much faster/better is the job done?|2. Rate Emotional impact 1-10: how much anxiety reduced or confidence gained?|3. Rate UX breakthrough 1-10: how much better vs current makeshift solution?|4. Rate Market scale 1-10: TAM bottom-up estimate supports viable business?|5. Score below 6 in any dimension = iterate on that dimension before proceeding
Best_For: Holistic idea scoring — catches ideas that are functional but lack emotional resonance or market scale
